title: Where the Gain Sits, and What It Costs

scenes.tts: Where exactly does a cascade get its gain? Follow one photon down the rod's ladder.
scenes.visual: Title card: Where the Gain Sits, and What It Costs. A photon at the top of a three-rung ladder. Question on screen: where is the gain?
scenes.narration: Where exactly does a cascade get its gain? Follow one photon down the rod's ladder.

scenes.tts: Step one. Activated rhodopsin switches on transducin, which switches on P D E six. Yue and colleagues counted each active unit as one effective complex.
scenes.caption: Step one. Activated rhodopsin switches on transducin, which switches on PDE6. Yue and colleagues counted each active unit as one effective complex.
scenes.visual: Rung 1 lights: activated rhodopsin, then transducin binding PDE6. A bracket groups them. Label: effective complex, a counting unit; its exact molecular make-up depends on the model.
scenes.narration: Step one. Activated rhodopsin switches on transducin, which switches on PDE6. Yue and colleagues counted each active unit as one effective complex.

scenes.tts: Step two. Each effective complex breaks down cyclic G M P, many molecules each.
scenes.caption: Step two. Each effective complex breaks down cyclic GMP, many molecules each.
scenes.visual: Rung 2 lights: each complex clears a patch of cGMP molecules around it.
scenes.narration: Step two. Each effective complex breaks down cyclic GMP, many molecules each.

scenes.tts: Step three. The fall in cyclic G M P closes cyclic nucleotide gated channels.
scenes.caption: Step three. The fall in cyclic GMP closes cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels.
scenes.visual: Rung 3 lights: channels in the outer membrane close as cGMP falls.
scenes.narration: Step three. The fall in cyclic GMP closes cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels.

scenes.tts: In mouse rods, about two thousand cyclic G M P molecules are hydrolysed for each absorbed photon.
scenes.caption: In mouse rods, about 2,000 cyclic GMP molecules are hydrolysed for each absorbed photon.
scenes.visual: Number on screen at the bottom of the ladder: about 2000 cGMP per photon, mouse rods (Arshavsky and Burns 2014).
scenes.narration: In mouse rods, about 2,000 cyclic GMP molecules are hydrolysed for each absorbed photon.

scenes.tts: In a separate study, Yue and colleagues estimated about twelve to fourteen effective complexes per activated rhodopsin.
scenes.caption: In a separate study, Yue and colleagues estimated about 12 to 14 effective complexes per activated rhodopsin.
scenes.visual: Number on screen beside rung 1: about 12 to 14 effective complexes per activated rhodopsin (Yue and colleagues 2019; Gcaps-null mouse rods).
scenes.narration: In a separate study, Yue and colleagues estimated about 12 to 14 effective complexes per activated rhodopsin.

scenes.tts: Predict. If these two estimates can be combined, which step multiplies the signal more?
scenes.visual: The ladder with two blank multiplier tags, one at rung 1 and one at rung 2. Small text: if the two estimates combine.
scenes.narration: Predict. If these two estimates can be combined, which step multiplies the signal more?

scenes.tts: If they combine, step two. Each complex would break down roughly a hundred and fifty molecules. That is an illustration, not a measured yield.
scenes.caption: If they combine, step two. Each complex would break down roughly 150 molecules. That is an illustration, not a measured yield.
scenes.visual: Tags fill in: about ×13 at rung 1 (Gcaps-null), roughly ×150 at rung 2, both marked: combination of separate estimates. One PDE6 complex cycles, cGMP entering and products leaving, over and over.
scenes.narration: If they combine, step two. Each complex would break down roughly 150 molecules. That is an illustration, not a measured yield.

scenes.tts: But other analyses put step one several times higher. On those, the two factors could be comparable.
scenes.visual: A dashed band over rung 1 labelled model-dependent estimates (Lamb 2022). The two tags move closer in size; both stay marked illustrative.
scenes.narration: But other analyses put step one several times higher. On those, the two factors could be comparable.

scenes.tts: Either way, both steps amplify. The gain belongs to particular enzymes, not to the receptor being a G protein coupled receptor.
scenes.visual: Text card: the gain belongs to particular enzymes, not to the label GPCR.
scenes.narration: Either way, both steps amplify. The gain belongs to particular enzymes, not to the receptor being a G protein coupled receptor.

scenes.tts: A receptor step need not amplify at all. In frog olfactory neurons, one bound receptor rarely activates even one G protein.
scenes.visual: Frog olfactory cilium: many bound receptors, most with no active G protein beside them. Label: Bhandawat, Reisert and Yau, 2005.
scenes.narration: A receptor step need not amplify at all. In frog olfactory neurons, one bound receptor rarely activates even one G protein.

scenes.tts: There, the gain is thought to come at later steps. Adenylyl cyclase makes cyclic A M P, which opens channels. The calcium that enters opens a chloride current.
scenes.caption: There, the gain is thought to come at later steps. Adenylyl cyclase makes cyclic AMP, which opens channels. The calcium that enters opens a chloride current.
scenes.visual: Adenylyl cyclase makes cAMP; cAMP opens cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels; calcium enters and opens a chloride channel beside them.
scenes.narration: There, the gain is thought to come at later steps. Adenylyl cyclase makes cyclic AMP, which opens channels. The calcium that enters opens a chloride current.

scenes.tts: Now the price. Every rung is an encounter between molecules, or an enzyme turning over. So the current rises only after several steps have run.
scenes.visual: The ladder with a small clock at each rung, the clocks of different sizes. Beside it, a direct channel whose current also rises over a finite time. Text: each step has its own rate; there is no fixed cost per rung.
scenes.narration: Now the price. Every rung is an encounter between molecules, or an enzyme turning over. So the current rises only after several steps have run.

scenes.tts: In mouse olfactory neurons, the earliest first spikes came about twenty five to forty milliseconds after a strong odour pulse.
scenes.caption: In mouse olfactory neurons, the earliest first spikes came about 25 to 40 milliseconds after a strong odour pulse.
scenes.visual: An odour pulse bar and a spike train below it, first spike marked. Label: earliest first spikes about 25 to 40 ms at high doses, dissociated mouse olfactory neurons (Ghatpande and Reisert 2011).
scenes.narration: In mouse olfactory neurons, the earliest first spikes came about 25 to 40 milliseconds after a strong odour pulse.

scenes.tts: That is a latency to a spike, which includes more than transduction. It is not a channel time constant.
scenes.visual: Tag on the spike latency: latency to a spike. Three small segments inside it: solution exchange, membrane charging, spike initiation.
scenes.narration: That is a latency to a spike, which includes more than transduction. It is not a channel time constant.

scenes.tts: Spontaneous receptor activity can also enter the cascade. Neurons with different odorant receptors showed different levels of spontaneous activity.
scenes.visual: Two olfactory-neuron baseline traces: one quiet, one noisy with spontaneous spikes. Label: Reisert 2010.
scenes.narration: Spontaneous receptor activity can also enter the cascade. Neurons with different odorant receptors showed different levels of spontaneous activity.

scenes.tts: Inverse agonist odorants could quiet it. A cascade that multiplies a receptor event multiplies a spontaneous one too.
scenes.visual: An inverse-agonist odorant arrives; the noisy trace quiets.
scenes.narration: Inverse agonist odorants could quiet it. A cascade that multiplies a receptor event multiplies a spontaneous one too.

scenes.tts: So enzymes between stimulus and pore can buy gain. They often pay in time, and they can amplify spontaneous activity too.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: What sits between the stimulus and the pore sets what a sensory cell can do. Enzyme cascades can amplify weak inputs and spontaneous upstream activity. Timing and signal-to-noise ratio depend on kinetics, feedback, filtering and where noise enters.
scenes.narration: So enzymes between stimulus and pore can buy gain. They often pay in time, and they can amplify spontaneous activity too.
